- [fact] If PURCHASE_UNITS.PAYMENT_INSTRUCTION.PLATFORM_FEES.PAYEE is not set, the fee amount will go to the live API caller account. — https://developer.paypal.com/platforms/overview
- [actionable] Set the refund amount during refund transactions using /v2/payments/captures/capture_id/refund in PAYMENT_INSTRUCTION.PLATFORM_FEES.AMOUNT. — https://developer.paypal.com/platforms/overview
- [fact] Partner must be enabled by PayPal to use the feature for setting refund amounts with partner fees. — https://developer.paypal.com/platforms/overview
- [idea] To receive money from partner fees, the platform fee payee must add a bank account to their PayPal account. — https://developer.paypal.com/platforms/overview
- [problem] If a partner wants to transact with the partner fees account as a seller or collect payments directly from buyers, it will cause issues. — https://developer.paypal.com/platforms/overview
- [idea] If the partner fees account causes transaction issues, the partner must make another account. — https://developer.paypal.com/platforms/overview

This token authenticates all SDK operations and is bound to your domain for security. This token expires after 15 minutes. You must generate a new token when needed. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/js/set-up#on-this-page
- [parameter] `components`: Required=no; Description=**string[].** An array of SDK components to load for your integration. Each component enables specific payment functionality. - [parameter] `pageType`: Required=no; Description=**string.** The type of page where the SDK is being initialized. This helps PayPal optimize the payment experience and provide better analytics. Accepted values: `checkout` — Checkout or payment page `product-details` — Individual product page `cart` — Shopping cart page `mini-cart` — Mini cart or side cart `home` — Homepage — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/js/set-up#on-this-page
- [parameter] `locale`: Required=no; Description=**string.** The locale for the UI components, specified as a BCP-47 language tag, for example,`"en-US"` ,`"fr-FR"` ,`"de-DE"` . - [concept] Push payments involve the payer sending money to a payee, while pull payments involve the payer authorizing the payee to debit funds from their account. — https://developer.paypal.com/payment-methods/
- [fact] Bank transfers are a type of push payment where the payer gives explicit instructions to their bank regarding amount and destination. — https://developer.paypal.com/payment-methods/
- [fact] Direct debits are a type of pull payment where the payee controls the amount and destination rather than the payer. — https://developer.paypal.com/payment-methods/
- [concept] Instant availability refers to near-immediate or immediate transfer of funds, whereas delayed availability involves a delay between initiation and completion. — https://developer.paypal.com/payment-methods/
- [fact] Faster Payment Service (FPS) in the UK and SEPA Instant Credit Transfers in the EU are examples of instant payment infrastructure for bank transfers. — https://developer.paypal.com/payment-methods/
- [fact] Voucher-based payments like Boleto are non-instant; funds are available immediately but the transaction is not instant because the payer completes payment offline later. — https://developer.paypal.com/payment-methods/
- [concept] Direct payments allow the payer to choose a method during checkout on the seller's page, while Redirect payments move the payer to the payment method's native experience. — https://developer.paypal.com/payment-methods/
- [fact] iDEAL is a redirect-based payment method that sends the payer to their bank's online banking environment to log in and approve the payment. — https://developer.paypal.com/payment-methods/
- [fact] Automated clearing house (ACH) transfers are a direct payment method where the payer stays on the same checkout page for the full journey. — https://developer.paypal.com/payment-methods/
- [fact] Boleto is an offline payment method requiring the payer to pay for a voucher at an authorized location like a convenience store or ATM. — https://developer.paypal.com/payment-methods/

- [fact] PayPal holds the disputed payment until resolution is reached. — https://developer.paypal.com/disputes/overview/

- [concept] An external dispute (or external case) is filed with a bank or card issuer, where the issuer manages adjudication and PayPal acts solely as an intermediary. — https://developer.paypal.com/disputes/overview/

- [concept] The inquiry stage begins with Item/Service Not Received (INR) or Significantly Not As Described (SNAD) issues, where parties can resolve directly or escalate to a claim. — https://developer.paypal.com/disputes/overview/
- [concept] The dispute resolution stage involves PayPal adjudicating internal disputes or the bank/card issuer adjudicating external disputes and communicating the outcome. — https://developer.paypal.com/disputes/overview/

- [actionable] Use the Disputes API to automate dispute management actions directly from your systems for scalable operations. — https://developer.paypal.com/disputes/overview/
- [fact] Both merchants and buyers can appeal unfavorable decisions after a dispute resolution. — https://developer.paypal.com/disputes/overview/
- [fact] If an internal dispute is resolved in the buyer's favor, PayPal refunds the transaction amount; if in the merchant's favor, PayPal releases the hold. — https://developer.paypal.com/disputes/overview/
- [fact] If an external dispute is resolved in the buyer's favor, the bank or card issuer refunds the transaction amount; if in the merchant's favor, it reverses the transaction. — https://developer.paypal.com/disputes/overview/

- [definition] Braintree Direct — Braintree Direct is a set of tools to accept and process cards, PayPal, and wallets such as Apple Pay, Google Pay, and Venmo (US only). It also includes everything you need to help prevent fraudulent transactions, manage data security, and streamline operations. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/#braintree-direct
- [definition] A sandbox account — As with any secure payment integration, you will first need to set up authorization. The Braintree sandbox allows you to set up a test environment to run transactions using test credit card numbers and explore the functionality of the Braintree gateway. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/#a-sandbox-account
- [definition] Client and server SDKs — Our client SDK enables you to securely collect payment information from your customers and the server SDK enables you to act on the collected payment information. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/#client-and-server-sdks
- [definition] Checkout UI — In this integration guide, we will use the [Drop-in UI](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/drop-in) for either web or mobile, based on the client and server SDK you choose. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/#checkout-ui
- [definition] Next up — We're glad you're here! Next, you'll integrate Braintree into your client. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/#next-up
- [fact] Starting September 1, 2026, the Drop-in SDK will be deprecated with no new features, improvements, or bug fixes released after this date. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/
- [fact] Payment processing for the Drop-in SDK will continue to be supported until September 1, 2027. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/
- [fact] Starting September 1, 2027, the Drop-in SDK will become unsupported and Braintree support team will no longer provide assistance. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/
- [problem] Payment processing for the Drop-in SDK may be suspended at any time after September 1, 2027. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/
- [actionable] Migrate to the Braintree Android SDK, Braintree iOS SDK, or Braintree JavaScript SDK to continue processing payments and receive ongoing updates. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/
- [concept] Braintree Direct is a set of tools to accept and process cards, PayPal, and wallets such as Apple Pay, Google Pay, and Venmo (US only). — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/
- [concept] The client SDK enables you to securely collect payment information from your customers. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/
- [concept] The server SDK enables you to act on the collected payment information. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/
- [fact] Client SDKs are available for Android, iOS, and JavaScript platforms. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/
- [fact] Server SDKs are available for Java, .NET, Node.js, PHP, Python, and Ruby languages. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/
- [concept] The client SDK requires authorization, typically using a client token which is the most flexible form of authorization. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/
- [idea] Use the Drop-in UI for web or mobile based on the chosen client and server SDK for basic integration. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/
- [idea] For more flexibility and customization, explore Hosted Fields for web or build a custom integration using iOS. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/
- [concept] The integration process begins with the front-end requesting a client token from the server to initialize the client SDK. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/
- [fact] In Step 2 of the integration, the server generates and sends a client token back to the client using the server SDK. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/
- [concept] In Step 3, the customer submits payment information which the client SDK communicates to Braintree to return a payment method nonce. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/
- [fact] In Step 4, the front-end sends the payment method nonce to the server. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/
- [concept] In Step 5, the server code receives the payment method nonce and uses the server SDK to create a transaction. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/start/overview/

## Overview
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/3d-secure/overview>

- [definition] Overview — Building a modern checkout experience requires that merchants balance security and ease of use for their customers. Coupled with strict regulatory requirements, 3D Secure (3DS) can help to prevent fraud and meet Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) requirements. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/3d-secure/overview#overview
- [definition] What's 3D Secure? — 3D Secure (3DS) is a security protocol designed to add an extra layer of security for online transactions. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/3d-secure/overview#whats-3d-secure
- [definition] What is SCA? — Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) is part of PSD2 regulations mandating that many transactions need to be carried out securely using at least 2 forms of customer authentication outlined in the PSD2 regulatory technical standards. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/3d-secure/overview#what-is-sca
- [definition] When is SCA required? — SCA is currently only required when both the acquirer and the issuer countries are both regulated by PSD2, such as countries in the EEA. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/3d-secure/overview#when-is-sca-required
- [definition] Payment flow — To make a 3D Secure call: - Generate a client token - Render a checkout page to collect customer payment information - Verify the credit card amount - The customer may then be prompted to authenticate if requested by the issuing bank, or otherwise required to do so by relevant local legislation — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/3d-secure/overview#payment-flow
- [concept] 3D Secure (3DS) is a security protocol that links the issuer, acquirer, and interoperability domains to authenticate transactions through an additional verification step. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/3d-secure/overview
- [fact] Liability for chargebacks on transactions verified through 3DS shifts from the merchant to the card issuer. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/3d-secure/overview
- [concept] Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) is a PSD2 regulatory requirement mandating at least two independent authentication factors for online transactions. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/3d-secure/overview
- [fact] The three SCA authentication factors are Knowledge (something you know), Possession (something you have), and Inherence (something you are). — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/3d-secure/overview
- [fact] SCA is required only when both the acquirer and issuer countries are regulated by PSD2, such as in the European Economic Area (EEA). — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/3d-secure/overview
- [problem] Merchants contracting with an acquirer licensed in a PSD2 country may see increased declines on transactions if SCA requirements are not met. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/3d-secure/overview
- [concept] 3DS2 is an iteration of the protocol that incorporates device information to improve risk assessment accuracy and reduce friction for mobile transactions. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/3d-secure/overview
- [fact] Supported card brand services include Visa Secure, MasterCard Identity Check, Discover ProtectBuy, and American Express SafeKey. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/3d-secure/overview
- [actionable] To make a 3D Secure call, generate a client token and render a checkout page to collect customer payment information. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/3d-secure/overview
- [actionable] If 3D Secure authentication is completed successfully or not required, use the returned nonce or authentication_id to create a transaction, customer, or payment method. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/3d-secure/overview
- [idea] Merchants should adopt 3DS to reduce fraud risk and meet Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) requirements. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/3d-secure/overview

- [parameter] **PayPal**: Client Token=Yes; Tokenization Key=Yes — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/authorization/overview#capabilities
- [parameter] **Apple Pay and Google Pay**: Client Token=Yes; Tokenization Key=Yes — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/authorization/overview#capabilities
- [parameter] **Venmo**: Client Token=Yes; Tokenization Key=Yes — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/authorization/overview#capabilities
- [parameter] **3D Secure**: Client Token=Yes; Tokenization Key=No — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/authorization/overview#capabilities
- [definition] Overview — Client SDKs require a form of authorization to interact with the Braintree gateway. The type of authorization you provide to your client determines what the client can do. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/authorization/overview#overview
- [definition] Types of authorization — We offer two forms of client authorization: - A tokenization key is a lightweight reusable value that authorizes payment method tokenization. - A client token is a short-lived value that authorizes payment method tokenization, payment method retrieval, and client-side vaulting. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/authorization/overview#types-of-authorization
- [definition] When to use tokenization keys — Tokenization keys do not require any interaction with your server until after payment information is tokenized. If you want to collect payment information to hand off to your server, tokenization keys are ideal. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/authorization/overview#when-to-use-tokenization-keys
- [definition] When to use client tokens — Client tokens allow use of the full range of Drop-in functionality. If you want customers to save their payment methods directly from your client or want to present returning customers with a list of their saved payment methods, use client tokens. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/authorization/overview#when-to-use-client-tokens
- [definition] Using both — If your client apps allow both guests and registered users to make purchases, you may wish to use both tokenization keys and client tokens. If this applies, instantiate a new Braintree instance with your authentication method of choice. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/authorization/overview#using-both

## Payment Method Nonces and Single-Use Payment Methods
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/payment-method-nonces>

- [definition] Payment Method Nonces and Single-Use Payment Methods — In the SDKs, a payment method nonce is a secure, one-time-use reference to payment information. It's the key element that allows your server to communicate sensitive payment information to Braintree without ever touching the raw data. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/payment-method-nonces#payment-method-nonces-and-single-use-payment-methods
- [definition] Payment method types — A single-use token can reference any payment method. This can help keep your integration simple and lightweight; for example, you could use the same server-side code for creating a PayPal transaction as you use for creating a credit card transaction. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/payment-method-nonces#payment-method-types
- [definition] Security — Security is important for all payment method types, but it's particularly critical for cards. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/payment-method-nonces#security
- [definition] Functionality — Braintree's servers will generate single-use tokens in response to requests from merchant clients and servers. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/payment-method-nonces#functionality
- [definition] Lifespan — A single-use token may only be used once. If it is not used, it expires 3 hours after being created. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/payment-method-nonces#lifespan
- [definition] Learn more — See more documentation on single-use tokens. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/payment-method-nonces#learn-more

## Add On
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/add-on>

- [concept] An add-on is a modification applied to a plan or subscription, distinguished by a specific value indicating whether it is an add-on or a discount. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/add-on
- [fact] The add-on amount attribute represents the monetary value of the add-on. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/add-on
- [fact] The creation date/time is returned in UTC format. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/add-on
- [fact] The billing cycle attribute increments each time the add-on is successfully applied. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/add-on
- [problem] For add-ons not attached to a subscription, the current billing cycle value will always be nil. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/add-on
- [fact] The description attribute contains text describing the add-on. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/add-on
- [problem] For add-ons attached to a subscription, the description value will always be nil. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/add-on
- [fact] The identifier is the unique token for the add-on. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/add-on
- [idea] Developers should note that the length and format of gateway-generated tokens and IDs may change at any time. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/add-on
- [fact] A specific value defines whether a modification is an add-on or a discount. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/add-on
- [problem] For add-ons attached to a subscription, the value distinguishing add-ons from discounts will always be nil. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/add-on
- [fact] The name attribute stores the name of the add-on. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/add-on
- [concept] A boolean value indicates whether an add-on's billing cycle is set to never expire rather than running for a specific number of cycles. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/add-on
- [fact] The number of billing cycles attribute specifies the duration of the add-on in billing cycles. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/add-on
- [problem] For add-ons not attached to a subscription, the count of times the add-on is applied will always be nil. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/add-on

- [definition] Code vs text — Most responses from Braintree will include both a code and text. The text is the human-readable description and the code is meant to be consumed programmatically. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices#code-vs-text
- [definition] Internet Explorer Quirks Mode — By writing invalid HTML syntax, you can cause versions of IE to enter Quirks Mode - a parsing mode that is designed to help render very old and/or invalid pages. Quirks Mode is unreliable and not supported by the JavaScript SDK, so the Drop-in UI may not appear in such cases. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices#internet-explorer-quirks-mode
- [definition] Minimum required server SDK versions — It goes without saying, but we'll say it anyway: we always recommend using the latest versions of our SDKs. While older versions may still be supported, in order to communicate securely with the Braintree gateway, you must use at least the version indicated below. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices#minimum-required-server-sdk-versions
- [definition] Timeouts — When using the server SDKs, keep in mind that some requests (like creating transactions) can take longer than expected since they rely on communicating with a payment processor. The Braintree gateway has a timeout of 60 seconds to accommodate for this. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices#timeouts
- [definition] Token and ID lengths and formats — In order to avoid interruptions in processing, it's best to make minimal assumptions about what our gateway-generated tokens and identifiers will look like in the future. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices#token-and-id-lengths-and-formats
- [definition] Transport Layer Security — Following the PCI Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) requirements, it's critical that you secure your connection to the Braintree gateway using Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.2 or higher, and serve any form that collects payment data in production over HTTPS. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices#transport-layer-security
- [definition] TLS Cipher Suites — In addition to ensuring you use TLS 1.2 or higher when connecting to Braintree, your integration must support at least one of the following TLS cipher suites. You must support at least one cipher suite for the version of TLS used by your integration. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices#tls-cipher-suites
- [definition] Testing — While you can successfully test our and over HTTP in all supported desktop and mobile browsers, you must use HTTPS if you wish to test our PayPal button in mobile webviews. Ultimately, we strongly encourage you to test all your flows over HTTPS to create a more realistic test environment. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices#testing
- [definition] SSL Certificates — We make periodic updates to our root SSL provider for API traffic to align with security standards. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices#ssl-certificates

- [parameter] `transmissionId`: The unique ID of the transmission, from the `paypal-transmission-id` HTTP header. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/#on-this-page
- [parameter] `timeStamp`: The date and time when the message was transmitted, from the `paypal-transmission-time` HTTP header. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/#on-this-page
- [parameter] `webhookId`: The ID of the webhook from when the listener URL subscribed to events. This does not come in the header or body of the message but rather where the webhook listener URL's event subscriptions are configured, such as [Application management](https://developer.paypal.com/dashboard/applications/) — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/#on-this-page
- [parameter] `crc32`: The [Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC32)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclic_redundancy_check) checksum for the body of the HTTP payload, in decimal form. You must use the original raw body to calculate this; do not parse the body to an array/object and then re-stringify it. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/#on-this-page
- [concept] There are two ways to subscribe a URL to webhook events: via Application management settings or programmatically using the Webhooks Management API. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/
- [fact] When subscribing a listener URL, it receives a unique Webhook ID that is required for verifying all webhook messages sent to that URL. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/
- [concept] A webhook listener must be an app or script deployed at a URL listening on HTTPS port 443 and must respond with an HTTP 2xx success status for every delivery. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/
- [fact] If a listener fails to respond or returns errors like 404 or 500, PayPal will retry each delivery up to 25 times over a period of 3 days. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/
- [actionable] Use the Webhooks simulator to generate mock events for development and testing purposes without belonging to any App. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/
- [fact] For signature verification of mock webhooks, the ID is the string `WEBHOOK_ID`, and postback verification to the verify-webhook-signature endpoint is not supported. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/
- [idea] Self cryptographic verification is the preferred method for systems that are programmatically capable as it is faster and avoids API dependency latency. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/
- [concept] To form the original message string for a signature check, concatenate `transmissionId`, `timeStamp`, `webhookId`, and `crc32` separated by pipes. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/
- [actionable] Utilize the public key from the certificate file specified by the header `paypal-cert-url` to validate the signature given by the header `paypal-transmission-sig`. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/
- [fact] The certificate file specified by `paypal-cert-url` should be automatically downloaded and cached for future use. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/
- [actionable] Alternatively, post the event back to the verify-webhook-signature REST API endpoint to have PayPal perform the verification instead of doing it yourself. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/
- [problem] Parsing webhook_event data to an array/object and re-serializing it back to a JSON string can fail verification; the data must be posted back exactly as received. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/
- [fact] After successfully receiving mock events, you must subscribe the listener URL to a sandbox REST App's events in Application management to generate actual test events. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/
- [problem] If PayPal cannot connect and receives no response, common causes include incoming HTTPS connections on port 443 being blocked by a firewall or the domain being marked as malware or phishing. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/
- [actionable] Check the status of your domain at urlfiltering.paloaltonetworks.com if you suspect it is marked as abusive or having malware. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/
- [problem] Receiving a non-2xx status code like 404 or 500 indicates a problem with the listener app/script or its webserver configuration that must be troubleshooted. — https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/webhooks/rest/

- [concept] SDK v2 replaces listener-based callbacks with sealed result types and requires explicit handling of 3D Secure auth challenges. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [fact] PayPal Native Payments are removed in SDK v2, with no replacement available for the discontinued native checkout dependency. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [fact] The migration does not require server-side changes or additional platform enrollment. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [problem] If `PayPalNativeClient` usage exists in the codebase, the project must be migrated to `PayPalWebCheckoutClient` before upgrading. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [actionable] Update `CardClient` and `PayPalWebCheckoutClient` constructors to accept a `Context` instead of an `Activity`. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [actionable] Remove all listener interfaces, listener assignments, and `removeObservers()` calls from the codebase. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [problem] The `removeObservers()` method does not exist in v2; leaving it in the code causes a compile error indicating remaining v1 references. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [actionable] Handle `AuthorizationRequired` results by calling `presentAuthChallenge()` when the SDK returns this state from `approveOrder()` or `vault()`. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [actionable] Dispatch pending card auth results in `onResume()` and `onNewIntent()` by calling `checkForCardAuthCompletion(newIntent)`. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [problem] Without calling `checkForCardAuthCompletion(newIntent)`, auth challenge completions arriving via `onNewIntent` are lost, leaving the buyer with no outcome. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [actionable] Dispatch pending PayPal auth results in `onResume()` and `onNewIntent()` by calling `checkForPayPalAuthCompletion(intent)`. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [fact] `PayPalPresentAuthChallengeResult.Success` only confirms the Chrome Custom Tab opened, not that the payment or vault was completed. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [actionable] Handle all four result states (`Success`, `Failure`, `Canceled`, and `NoResult`) in both `onResume()` and `onNewIntent()` for both clients. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [problem] Leaving the `PayPalNativePayments` module in `build.gradle` alongside v2 artifacts causes a build failure. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [actionable] Set `Environment.SANDBOX` in `CoreConfig` and create sandbox buyer accounts for testing before upgrading to live. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [idea] Log the `debug_id` from any SDK errors to facilitate escalation to PayPal support. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [fact] The solution availability depends on the user's country or territory before upgrading. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [actionable] Ensure the deep link scheme is registered in `AndroidManifest.xml` with a production intent filter before release. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [problem] If the project still uses the single-argument v1 signature for `start()` or `vault()`, a compile error will identify call sites needing updates. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android
- [fact] In v2, the SDK lifecycle observer no longer automatically processes intents in `onNewIntent`; manual calls are required. — https://developer.paypal.com/sdk/update-android

## Payment API Concepts
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/concepts/>

- [definition] Payment API Concepts — This guide contains additional context on the main types in the Braintree API and their behavior. Check out the [API Explorer](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/explorer) for a full list and documentation of all possible fields on each object type covered here. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/concepts/#payment-api-concepts
- [definition] The Lifecycle of a Payment — Braintree offers APIs and SDKs to collect payment from customer checkout all the way to funds settling in your bank account. The typical payment lifecycle looks something like this: 1. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/concepts/#the-lifecycle-of-a-payment
- [definition] Payment Methods — A `PaymentMethod` is how Braintree represents **any single thing a customer could use to pay for something**, such as a credit card (either directly or via a wallet like Apple Pay or Google Pay), a PayPal account, a Venmo account, or a bank account. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/concepts/#payment-methods
- [definition] The Braintree Vault — Your Vault is where we securely store your customers' payment data long-term, allowing you to charge repeat customers without making them re-enter their payment information. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/concepts/#the-braintree-vault
- [definition] Transactions — Transactions are produced when you charge a payment method. A `Transaction` represents **the (attempted) movement of money from a customer to you to pay for something**. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/concepts/#transactions
- [definition] Transactions and Payment Methods — The `Transaction` type has two fields to represent the payment method transacted against: `paymentMethodSnapshot` and `paymentMethod`. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/concepts/#transactions-and-payment-methods
- [definition] Customers — Customers are an optional component of the API that provide a way to store personal information about anyone who holds a vaulted payment method or initiates a transaction. Customers can be used to group payment methods and transactions, and have a one-to-many relationship with both. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/concepts/#customers

There are different types of credentials you can use to authorize depending on what you'd like to do. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/making_api_calls/#the-authorization-header
- [definition] The Braintree-Version Header — You MUST provide a `Braintree-Version` header with a date in the format `YYYY-MM-DD`. We recommend using the date on which you begin integrating with the GraphQL API. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/making_api_calls/#the-braintree-version-header
- [definition] The Content-Type Header — The content type of a query MUST be `application/json`. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/making_api_calls/#the-content-type-header
- [definition] The Message Body — The message body MUST be a JSON object. It MUST contain a `query` key and MAY contain a `variables` key. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/making_api_calls/#the-message-body
- [definition] Your First Request — The simplest request is `ping`. It is mainly useful to ensure you understand how to generate well-formed requests. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/making_api_calls/#your-first-request
- [definition] A More Interesting Request — Here is a typical request body for the `chargePaymentMethod` mutation (Note: we have added newlines for readability but normally, [JSON strings](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7159#section-7) MUST escape newlines): — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/making_api_calls/#a-more-interesting-request
- [definition] Two Mutations In One Call — By using [GraphQL aliases](https://graphql.org/learn/queries/#aliases), we can make multiple charges in a single call to the API: 1. RequestBody 2. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/making_api_calls/#two-mutations-in-one-call
- [definition] Understanding Responses — A response from the GraphQL API will always return with HTTP status 200. The JSON body of the response explains whether an error occurred. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/making_api_calls/#understanding-responses
- [definition] Data — A successful query MUST return a JSON object with a `data` key whose value is a JSON object with the data you requested. Each key in the data object will exactly match those specified in the query. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/making_api_calls/#data
- [definition] Errors — Unlike a conventional REST API, GraphQL APIs do not rely on HTTP status codes to signal request outcomes. Our GraphQL API always return a JSON body with the `200` status code, even when there are errors. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/making_api_calls/#errors
- [definition] Extensions — The API response MUST contain an `extensions` object. This object contains at least a `requestId` entry that is unique to the request and useful to Braintree Support should you need help debugging a request. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/making_api_calls/#extensions
- [definition] Timeouts — When using the GraphQL API, keep in mind that some requests (like creating transactions) can take longer than expected since they rely on communicating with a payment processor. We set a recommend setting a timeout of 60 seconds to accommodate for this. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/making_api_calls/#timeouts
- [definition] Using GraphiQL — We've integrated the [GraphiQL](https://github.com/graphql/graphiql) project into our GraphQL documentation to allow you to explore the API in your browser using your sandbox API credentials. GraphiQL is a graphical interactive IDE for exploring and playing around with GraphQL APIs. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/making_api_calls/#using-graphiql

## Overview
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/overview/>

- [definition] Overview — We offer a variety of products that make it easy for you to accept payments in your app or website. Think of us as the credit card terminal you swipe your card through at the grocery store. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/overview/#overview
- [definition] Business bank account — We’ll deposit your funds into this account automatically – it’s up to you to decide which institution you use for your business’s bank account. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/overview/#business-bank-account
- [definition] Merchant account — A merchant account is not a bank account – it's what we use to route funds from your customers’ accounts to your business bank account. We provide a merchant account as a part of the setup. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/overview/#merchant-account
- [definition] Payment gateway — Braintree’s payment gateway will connect you to all of the banking institutions and payment processors that you need in order to collect money from your customers. You’ll give the payment information to Braintree, and we’ll let you know if the transaction was approved by the bank. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/overview/#payment-gateway
- [definition] Developer knowledge — Integrating with a payment gateway is a developer’s job. ## Payment Methods
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/payment-methods>

- [definition] Payment Methods — Integrating with Braintree offers your customers many different ways to pay – and we’re always working on adding more. Here's a quick list of what we currently offer, and whom they are available to. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/payment-methods#payment-methods
- [definition] ACH Direct Debit — Most merchants in the US can accept ACH Direct Debit transactions from participating customers. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/payment-methods#ach-direct-debit
- [definition] Apple Pay — Most merchants located in the US, Canada, Europe, Australia, and APAC regions can accept Apple Pay transactions from participating customers – depending on your processor settings. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/payment-methods#apple-pay
- [definition] Google Pay — Most merchants located in the US, Canada, Europe, Australia, and APAC regions can accept Google Pay transactions from participating customers – with approval from Google. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/payment-methods#google-pay
- [definition] Credit cards — Braintree’s US merchant accounts bundle Visa, Mastercard, Discover, UnionPay, JCB, and sometimes American Express as the default accepted payment types. Most of our international merchant accounts bundle Visa and Mastercard as the default accepted payment types. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/payment-methods#credit-cards
- [definition] Debit cards — When processing payments online, credit and debit cards are handled the same, as long as they are issued by a major card brand. Because PINs can't be accepted online, debit cards will always be run as credit. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/payment-methods#debit-cards
- [definition] Dual-branded cards — Dual-branded cards include two different card brand logos and can be processed through either brand's network. Merchants can process these cards on whichever network is supported in their region. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/payment-methods#dual-branded-cards
- [definition] Special-use cards — Credit and debit cards issued for specific purchases – like or [P-Cards](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purchasing_card) – can only be accepted if your merchant account is associated with the appropriate MCC (Merchant Category Code). — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/payment-methods#special-use-cards
- [definition] PayPal — Braintree is the only payment platform that allows you to accept both cards **and** PayPal through a single integration. PayPal is available to most of our merchants. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/payment-methods#paypal
- [definition] Local Payment Methods — In addition to PayPal and cards, you can now offer the most relevant Local Payment Methods for your customers with a single Braintree integration. This will allow your cross-border customers to pay in their preferred Local Payment Methods while all payments settle into your PayPal account. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/payment-methods#local-payment-methods
- [definition] Venmo — Venmo allows customers on iOS and Android devices or on the desktop site to connect their Venmo account to your mobile app or desktop website – making it easy for them to make purchases using their bank account, credit and debit cards, or Venmo balance. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/payment-methods#venmo
- [definition] Secure Remote Commerce — Secure Remote Commerce (SRC) is a digital wallet that allows customers to store all of their major debit and credit cards in one account. With this single sign-in experience through Visa, customers can easily make purchases on your website or mobile app using any of the cards saved in their wallet. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/payment-methods#secure-remote-commerce

## Transaction Lifecycle
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/transaction-lifecycle>

- [definition] Transaction Lifecycle — As money travels from the customer to your bank account, the transaction is given a series of statuses. A **successful** transaction will go through the following statuses: Transaction statuses can help you understand where your money is in the transaction lifecycle. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/transaction-lifecycle#transaction-lifecycle
- [definition] Authorized — When a purchase is first submitted by a customer, we start by checking with the customer’s bank to see if the payment method is legitimate and has sufficient funds to pay for your product or service. If the customer's bank approves, the transaction will be given an *Authorized* status. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/transaction-lifecycle#authorized
- [definition] Submitted for Settlement — Eventually, authorizations will expire. In order to collect funds, a transaction needs to be submitted for settlement – which happens by default when creating transactions via the Control Panel. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/transaction-lifecycle#submitted-for-settlement
- [definition] Settling — When we begin communicating with the processor about the settlement request, the transaction will move from *Submitted for Settlement* to *Settling*. The amount of time a transaction spends in the *Settling* state depends on the processing bank. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/transaction-lifecycle#settling
- [definition] Settled — This is when the money moves from your customer’s bank through your merchant account. Once the money hits your merchant account, the transaction will display as *Settled*, and the funds will be routed to your bank account. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/transaction-lifecycle#settled
- [definition] Other statuses — If the transaction is unsuccessful, or is interrupted in some way, there are other transaction statuses that can indicate what is happening. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/get-started/transaction-lifecycle#other-statuses

## ACH Direct Debit
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/payment-methods/ach>

- [definition] ACH Direct Debit — ACH, or Automated Clearing House, is a payment method that runs on banking networks in the United States. It allows customers to pay for transactions by debiting directly from their bank account, as opposed to processing through a card brand. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/payment-methods/ach#ach-direct-debit
- [definition] Availability — ACH Direct Debit is available for merchants who: - Are located in the United States - Transact in the US in USD - Are processing with Braintree Direct - Are in good standing (i.e. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/payment-methods/ach#availability
- [definition] Verification methods — For ACH Direct Debit, you're required to verify a bank account before collecting money from it. Verifications provide a way for you to check the validity of a bank account before attempting to process a transaction – helping you protect yourself against fraudulent or erroneous transactions. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/payment-methods/ach#verification-methods
- [definition] Instant verification — Verifies a customer's U.S. bank account in real time through secure open banking connections. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/payment-methods/ach#instant-verification
- [definition] Network check — Network check instantly verifies your customer's bank account by requiring entry of specific account information (such as routing number and account number) at checkout. While network check provides near-instantaneous verification, it is not supported by all banks. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/payment-methods/ach#network-check
- [definition] Micro-transfers — Micro-transfers require your customer to first enter their bank account information (e.g. routing number, account number), and then confirm the amounts of two deposits we send to their provided account in a custom UI built by your developers. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/payment-methods/ach#micro-transfers
- [definition] Independent check — If you'd like to manually manage verification, you can do so with independent check. There are two options: - Collect physically voided checks to verify the account - Use another third-party verification provider — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/payment-methods/ach#independent-check
- [definition] Business versus personal bank accounts — If you choose to verify bank accounts using the network check, micro-transfers, or independent check methods, one of the fields we require you to collect is the *account ownership type*, which can be either business or personal. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/payment-methods/ach#business-versus-personal-bank-accounts
- [definition] PayPal Company ID and Company Name — Another reason for a return may be that your customer has a debit block in place. If a transaction is returned for this reason, you'll be charged a return fee and will need to ask your customer to call their bank to get the debit block lifted from their bank account. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/payment-methods/ach#paypal-company-id-and-company-name
- [definition] Processing — ACH is a batch-based system, meaning that transactions do not take place in real-time, and authorizations or captures do not exist as they do with credit card transactions. This makes it more difficult to verify whether funds will be available in the account at the time the transaction takes place. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/payment-methods/ach#processing
- [definition] Settlement and funding timeline — Before we disburse funds to your account, we wait for 3 business days for any returns that the customer's bank sends through the ACH network. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/payment-methods/ach#settlement-and-funding-timeline
- [definition] Fees — Transactions processed with ACH have an additional processing fee, which can be found in your pricing agreement. A $5 USD fee will be charged for any returns or disputes. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/payment-methods/ach#fees
- [definition] Voids and Refunds — ACH transactions can't be voided at any point in the transaction lifecycle. Refunds can be processed, but only on transactions with the Settled status. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/payment-methods/ach#voids-and-refunds
- [definition] Returns — ACH transactions can be returned for a variety of reasons. Although a majority of returns are received in 3 business days, returns can be received after disbursement. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/payment-methods/ach#returns
- [definition] Blocked Bank Accounts — To comply with NACHA rules and minimize fraud, return fees, and other risks, we block bank accounts that receive certain ACH return codes. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/payment-methods/ach#blocked-bank-accounts
- [definition] Disputes — Customers can report disputes to their bank for unauthorized transactions – commonly referred to as unauths. This window varies depending on the type of bank account they have. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/payment-methods/ach#disputes
- [definition] Setup — To add ACH Direct Debit to your Braintree integration, you'll need to update your application code and make sure ACH Direct Debit is enabled in your Control Panel. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/payment-methods/ach#setup

Because you have a different set of API keys for each environment, you'll need to update your code depending on which environment you're working in. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/control-panel/important-gateway-credentials#environment
- [definition] API keys — The public and private keys together make up your user's API keys. - [definition] Merchant ID — Your merchant ID is not the same as your merchant account ID. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/control-panel/important-gateway-credentials#merchant-id
- [definition] Additional credentials — Depending on your integration, you may need to provide other credentials in addition to those listed above. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/control-panel/important-gateway-credentials#additional-credentials
- [definition] Merchant account ID — Your merchant account ID is not the same as your merchant ID. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/control-panel/important-gateway-credentials#merchant-account-id
- [definition] Tokenization keys — [Tokenization keys](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/authorization/tokenization-key) can be used for authorization in your Braintree integration. They authorize the client SDK to tokenize payment information for use on your server. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/control-panel/important-gateway-credentials#tokenization-keys
- [definition] Client-Side Encryption key — The Client-Side Encryption (CSE) key is required if you are using our older integration method. Similar to the merchant ID, this value is unique to your entire Braintree gateway account, not to a specific user. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/control-panel/important-gateway-credentials#client-side-encryption-key

## Overview

- [definition] Overview — Merchant account providers like Braintree are financially liable for all merchant losses. - [definition] Risk factors — Certain business models are considered to be higher risk than others based on decades of credit card processing data. - [definition] How we mitigate risk — We can sometimes minimize our financial exposure enough to allow merchants with high-risk business models to process with us. - [definition] Require a personal or corporate guarantee — After reviewing your company’s financials, we will sometimes require a personal or corporate guarantee. Because we bear all financial liability, we want to make sure that owners have similar incentives to deliver their products or services. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/overview#require-a-personal-or-corporate-guarantee
- [definition] Establish a reserve — Depending on the risk involved with your business model, we might hold funds in a reserve to ensure that we can cover refunds and chargebacks if you are unable to. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/overview#establish-a-reserve

To simulate unsuccessful API calls in Sandbox, check out our — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/merchant-account/#unsuccessful-result

## AVS and CVV Response Codes
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/>

- [parameter] Postal Code matches (M): The postal code provided matches the information on file with the cardholder's bank. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#avs
- [parameter] Postal Code does not match (N): The postal code provided does not match the information on file with the cardholder's bank. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#avs
- [parameter] Postal Code not verified (U): The card-issuing bank received the postal code but did not verify whether it was correct. This typically happens if the processor declines an authorization before the bank evaluates the postal code. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#avs
- [parameter] Postal Code not provided (I): No postal code was provided. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#avs
- [parameter] Street Address matches (M): The street address provided matches the information on file with the cardholder's bank. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#avs
- [parameter] Street Address does not match (N): The street address provided does not match the information on file with the cardholder's bank. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#avs
- [parameter] Street Address not verified (U): The card-issuing bank received the street address but did not verify whether it was correct. This typically happens if the processor declines an authorization before the bank evaluates the address. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#avs
- [parameter] Street Address not provided (I): No street address was provided. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#avs
- [parameter] Issuing bank does not support AVS (S): AVS information was provided but the card-issuing bank does not participate in address verification. This typically indicates a card-issuing bank outside of the US, Canada, and the UK. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#avs
- [parameter] AVS system error (E): A system error prevented any verification of street address or postal code. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#avs
- [parameter] AVS not applicable (A): AVS information was provided but this type of transaction does not support address verification. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#avs
- [parameter] AVS skipped (B): AVS checks were skipped for this transaction. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#avs
- [parameter] CVV matches (M): The CVV provided matches the information on file with the cardholder's bank. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#cvv
- [parameter] CVV does not match (N): The CVV provided does not match the information on file with the cardholder's bank. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#cvv
- [parameter] CVV is not verified (U): The card-issuing bank received the CVV, but did not verify whether it was correct. This typically happens if the bank declines an authorization before evaluating the CVV. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#cvv
- [parameter] CVV not provided (I): No CVV was provided. This also happens if the transaction was made with a vaulted payment         method. [Learn more about AVS and CVV rules in the Vault.](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/fraud-tools/basic/avs-cvv-rules#avs-and-cvv-rules-in-the-vault) — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#cvv
- [parameter] Issuer does not participate (S): The CVV was provided but the card-issuing bank does not participate in card verification. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#cvv
- [parameter] CVV not applicable (A): The CVV was provided but this type of transaction does not support card verification. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#cvv
- [parameter] CVV skipped (B): CVV checks were skipped for this transaction. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#cvv
- [definition] AVS and CVV Response Codes — Available on the[Credit Card Verification](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/credit-card-verification/ruby)[Transaction](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/transaction/ruby) — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/processor-responses/avs-cvv-responses/#avs-and-cvv-response-codes

## Search Fields
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/searching/search-fields/>

- [snippet] Text fields: search_results = gateway.transaction.search do |search| — `search_results = gateway.transaction.search do |search|` — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/searching/search-fields/#text-fields
- [snippet] Multiple value fields: search_results = gateway.transaction.search do |search| — `search_results = gateway.transaction.search do |search|` — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/searching/search-fields/#multiple-value-fields
- [snippet] Range fields: search_results = gateway.transaction.search do |search| — `search_results = gateway.transaction.search do |search|` — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/searching/search-fields/#range-fields
- [definition] Search Fields — We support three types of search fields: - Text fields - Multiple value fields - Range fields — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/searching/search-fields/#search-fields
- [definition] Text fields — Text Fields can be searched using 5 operators: `is`, `is_not`, `starts_with`, `ends_with`, and `contains`. Each search Text Field can't exceed 255 characters. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/searching/search-fields/#text-fields
- [definition] Multiple value fields — Search fields that accept multiple values support two operators: `is` and `in`. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/searching/search-fields/#multiple-value-fields
- [definition] Range fields — Ranges support four operators: `is`, `between`, `>=`, and `<=`. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/searching/search-fields/#range-fields

## Search Results
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/searching/search-results/>

- [snippet] Maximum size: search_results = gateway.transaction.search do |search| — `search_results = gateway.transaction.search do |search|` — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/searching/search-results/#maximum-size
- [definition] Search Results — `Enumerable` so you can iterate over them using `each` or any method — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/searching/search-results/#search-results
- [definition] Race conditions — To optimize the processing of large searches, data is retrieved from the server *lazily*. Initially, the server returns a list of ids that matched the search criteria. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/searching/search-results/#race-conditions
- [definition] Records are deleted — If a record is deleted server-side while you are iterating over the results, that record is *skipped*. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/searching/search-results/#records-are-deleted
- [definition] Records are updated — If a record is updated server-side while you are iterating over the results, one of two things could happen: - the record still matches the search criteria and the modified record is *returned* - the record no longer matches the search criteria and is *skipped* — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/searching/search-results/#records-are-updated
- [definition] Maximum size — Because of the race conditions described above, you can't know how many search results you have while iterating over them. You do, however, know the maximum number of results that will be given. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/searching/search-results/#maximum-size

## Server SDK Migration Guide
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/server-sdk-migration-guide/>

- [definition] Overview — Braintree makes regular updates to our server SDKs which follow [semantic versioning](https://semver.org/) guidelines. This page will guide you through the largest breaking changes that are specific to the language you are integrating with Braintree. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/server-sdk-migration-guide/#overview
- [definition] Ruby versions — Previous versions of the Ruby SDK supported older, now End-of-Life versions of Ruby. Starting with version 4.0.0, the Braintree Ruby SDK only supports Ruby versions 2.6+. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/server-sdk-migration-guide/#ruby-versions
- [definition] XML parsing — Version 3 of the Ruby SDK required `libxml-ruby`. In version 4, `libxml-ruby` is an optional dependency that can be included for more performant XML parsing. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/server-sdk-migration-guide/#xml-parsing
- [definition] Ruby versions — Previous versions of the Ruby SDK supported older, now End-of-Life versions of Ruby. Starting with version 3.0.1, the Braintree Ruby SDK only supports Ruby versions 2.5+. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/server-sdk-migration-guide/#ruby-versions
- [definition] Google Pay — Previous versions of the Ruby SDK represented Google Pay cards as Android Pay cards to prevent breaking changes. In version 3.0.1, `AndroidPayCard` and `AndroidPayCardDetails` were renamed to `GooglePayCard` and `GooglePayCardDetails`. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/server-sdk-migration-guide/#google-pay
- [definition] Exceptions — Down For Maintenance exceptions have been renamed to Service Unavailable exceptions, since we do not bring our services down to perform maintenance operations anymore. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/server-sdk-migration-guide/#exceptions

## Statuses
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/>

- [parameter] Visa **¹**: Transaction type=Default; Time before expiration=8 days — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#authorization-expired
- [parameter] Mastercard **²**: Transaction type=Preauthorization; Time before expiration=30 days — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#authorization-expired
- [parameter] American Express: Transaction type=Default; Time before expiration=7 days — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#authorization-expired
- [parameter] Lodging & Cruise Lines: Time before expiration=30 days — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#authorization-expired
- [parameter] Discover Diners Club UnionPay JCB: Transaction type=Default; Time before expiration=30 days — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#authorization-expired
- [parameter] PayPal: Transaction type=Default; Time before expiration=29 days — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#authorization-expired
- [parameter] Pay with Venmo: Transaction type=Default; Time before expiration=10 days — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#authorization-expired
- [definition] Authorized — The processor authorized the transaction. Your customer may see a pending charge on his or her account. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#authorized
- [definition] Authorization expired — The transaction spent too much time in the *Authorized* status and was marked as expired. Expiration time frames differ by payment instrument subtype, transaction type, and, in some cases, merchant category. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#authorization-expired
- [definition] Processor declined — The processor declined the transaction. The has information about why the transaction was declined. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#processor-declined
- [definition] Gateway rejected — The gateway rejected the transaction because [risk threshold](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/fraud-tools/basic/risk-threshold-rules), or checks failed, or because you have on your provisional merchant account. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#gateway-rejected
- [definition] Failed — An error occurred when sending the transaction to the processor. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#failed
- [definition] Voided — The transaction was voided. You can when the status is *Authorized*, *Submitted for Settlement*, or – in the case of – *Settlement Pending*. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#voided
- [definition] Submitted for settlement — The transaction has been submitted for settlement and will be included in the next settlement batch. Settlement happens nightly – the exact time depends on the processor. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#submitted-for-settlement
- [definition] Settling — The transaction is in the process of being settled. This is a transitory state. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#settling
- [definition] Settlement declined — The processor declined to settle the sale or refund request, and the result is unsuccessful. This can happen for a number of reasons, but the may have more information about why the transaction was declined. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#settlement-declined
- [definition] Settlement pending — The transaction has not yet fully settled. This status is rare, and it does not always indicate a problem with settlement. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#settlement-pending
- [definition] Settlement confirmed — The transaction was captured partially. The parent transaction will not be submitted to the processor for settling, and will transition to `settlement_confirmed`. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#settlement-confirmed
- [definition] Processor declined — The processor declined the verification. The has information about why the verification was declined. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#processor-declined
- [definition] Gateway rejected — The gateway rejected the verification because [duplicate](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/control-panel/transactions/duplicate-checking), or [fraud](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/fraud-tools/overview) checks failed, or because you have on your provisional… — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#gateway-rejected
- [definition] Failed — An error occurred when sending the verification to the processor. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#failed
- [definition] Verified — The card was verified successfully by the processor. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#verified
- [definition] Accepted — You have opted out of providing evidence for the chargeback or pre-arb. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#accepted
- [definition] Auto Accepted — The dispute has been automatically accepted for the best merchant experience. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#auto-accepted
- [definition] Disputed — Evidence has been submitted to the customer's bank for evaluation. No action is needed at this time. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#disputed
- [definition] Expired — The reply-by date to submit evidence has passed and you have forfeited your right to respond to the case. This includes disputes that were accepted on your behalf because you did not respond. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#expired
- [definition] Lost — The bank evaluated the dispute and ruled in the customer’s favor. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#lost
- [definition] Open — The chargeback, retrieval, or pre-arb has been issued and no action has been taken yet. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#open
- [definition] Under Review — Your case is under internal review with PayPal. No action is needed at this time. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#under-review
- [definition] Won — The bank evaluated the dispute and ruled in your favor. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#won
- [definition] Hold pending — The transaction will be held in escrow once settled. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#hold-pending
- [definition] Held — The transaction has settled and is now held in escrow and eligible to be released. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#held
- [definition] Release pending — The transaction being held in escrow will be released and disbursed shortly. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#release-pending
- [definition] Released — The transaction that was being held in escrow has been released. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#released
- [definition] Refunded — The transaction that was being held in escrow has been refunded. Only full refunds are allowed for escrow transactions. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#refunded
- [definition] Pending — *Pending* subscriptions are subscriptions that have not started yet. For example, if you create a subscription with a specific billing date in the future, the subscription will start out as *Pending*. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#pending
- [definition] Active — *Active* subscriptions will be charged on the next billing date. You can get the dates from the [subscription object](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/response/subscription). — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#active
- [definition] Past Due — We can send email notifications to your customers when their subscription becomes past due. See our for more information. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#past-due
- [definition] Expired — Subscriptions are *Expired* when they have reached the specified — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#expired
- [definition] Canceled — If you the subscription, the status will be *Canceled* and no further billing will occur. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/statuses/#canceled
