- [parameter] Sandbox: URL=api.sandbox.braintreegateway.com; Date Implemented=February 2025; Certificates=[Click here to download certificate files](https://paypalobjects.com/ppdevdocs/api.sandbox.braintreegateway.com.zip) — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices/java/#ssl-certificates
- [parameter] Production: URL=api.braintreegateway.com; Date Implemented=September 2025; Certificates=[Click here to download certificate files](https://paypalobjects.com/ppdevdocs/api.braintreegateway.com.zip) — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices/java/#ssl-certificates
- [definition] Best Practices — The SSL certificates for Braintree Mobile (iOS and Android) SDKs are set to expire on March 30, 2026. This will impact published versions of your app if they utilize older versions of the SDK. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices/java/#best-practices
- [definition] Autocomplete — When building a web form that has an input for a credit card number, turn off autocomplete so that your customer's browser won't save their credit card number. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices/java/#autocomplete
- [definition] Code vs text — Most responses from Braintree will include both a code and text. The text is the human-readable description and the code is meant to be consumed programmatically. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices/java/#code-vs-text
- [definition] Internet Explorer Quirks Mode — By writing invalid HTML syntax, you can cause versions of IE to enter Quirks Mode - a parsing mode that is designed to help render very old and/or invalid pages. Quirks Mode is unreliable and not supported by the JavaScript SDK, so the Drop-in UI may not appear in such cases. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices/java/#internet-explorer-quirks-mode
- [definition] Minimum required server SDK versions — It goes without saying, but we'll say it anyway: we always recommend using the latest versions of our SDKs. While older versions may still be supported, in order to communicate securely with the Braintree gateway, you must use at least the version indicated below. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices/java/#minimum-required-server-sdk-versions
- [definition] Check your current server SDK version — To verify which version of the Braintree Java SDK you're currently using, see the instructions for Maven or JAR files below. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices/java/#check-your-current-server-sdk-version
- [definition] Upgrade your server SDK version — See the [Braintree Java version changelog](https://github.com/braintree/braintree_java/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md) . — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices/java/#upgrade-your-server-sdk-version
- [definition] Timeouts — When using the server SDKs, keep in mind that some requests (like creating transactions) can take longer than expected since they rely on communicating with a payment processor. The Braintree gateway has a timeout of 60 seconds to accommodate for this. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices/java/#timeouts
- [definition] Token and ID lengths and formats — In order to avoid interruptions in processing, it's best to make minimal assumptions about what our gateway-generated tokens and identifiers will look like in the future. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices/java/#token-and-id-lengths-and-formats
- [definition] Transport Layer Security — Following the PCI Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) requirements, it's critical that you secure your connection to the Braintree gateway using Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.2 or higher, and serve any form that collects payment data in production over HTTPS. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/reference/general/best-practices/java/#transport-layer-security

- [definition] Use Open Authorization (OAuth) 2.0 for all API authentication [#use-open-authorization-oauth-20-for-all-api-authentication] — PayPal uses OAuth 2.0 as the standard authentication mechanism for all REST API integrations. OAuth 2.0 provides secure, token-based authentication, allowing applications to access PayPal APIs without exposing user credentials. — https://developer.paypal.com/security-guidelines.md#use-open-authorization-oauth-20-for-all-api-authentication-use-open-authorization-oauth-20-for-all-api-authentication
- [definition] Always use HTTPS for all API and SDK requests [#always-use-https-for-all-api-and-sdk-requests] — All communication with PayPal APIs and SDKs must use HTTPS to ensure data is encrypted in transit and protected from interception or tampering. HTTPS is required for PCI DSS compliance and is enforced by PayPal for all endpoints. — https://developer.paypal.com/security-guidelines.md#always-use-https-for-all-api-and-sdk-requests-always-use-https-for-all-api-and-sdk-requests
- [definition] Never expose your client secret or API credentials in client-side code [#never-expose-your-client-secret-or-api-credentials-in-client-side-code] — Your client secret and API credentials must always be kept confidential and used only on the server side. Exposing these credentials in client-side cod, such as JavaScript running in the browser, can lead to credential theft and unauthorized access to your PayPal account. — https://developer.paypal.com/security-guidelines.md#never-expose-your-client-secret-or-api-credentials-in-client-side-code-never-expose-your-client-secret-or-api-credentials-in-client-side-code
- [definition] Store credentials securely using environment variables or secure vaults [#store-credentials-securely-using-environment-variables-or-secure-vaults] — Sensitive credentials should be stored in environment variables or secure vaults, not in source code or configuration files. This reduces the risk of accidental exposure through version control or code sharing. — https://developer.paypal.com/security-guidelines.md#store-credentials-securely-using-environment-variables-or-secure-vaults-store-credentials-securely-using-environment-variables-or-secure-vaults
- [definition] Rotate API credentials regularly and remove unused credentials [#rotate-api-credentials-regularly-and-remove-unused-credentials] — Regularly rotating your API credentials and removing any that are no longer in use minimizes the risk if credentials are ever compromised. — https://developer.paypal.com/security-guidelines.md#rotate-api-credentials-regularly-and-remove-unused-credentials-rotate-api-credentials-regularly-and-remove-unused-credentials
- [definition] Validate all webhook signatures to ensure authenticity [#validate-all-webhook-signatures-to-ensure-authenticity] — Always verify webhook signatures using PayPal's verification API before processing events. This ensures the event is genuine and untampered, protecting your application from spoofed or malicious notifications. — https://developer.paypal.com/security-guidelines.md#validate-all-webhook-signatures-to-ensure-authenticity-validate-all-webhook-signatures-to-ensure-authenticity
- [definition] Keep all dependencies, SDKs, and libraries up to date [#keep-all-dependencies-sdks-and-libraries-up-to-date] — Regularly update all dependencies, SDKs, and libraries to patch security vulnerabilities and benefit from the latest security improvements. Outdated software can expose your application to known exploits. — https://developer.paypal.com/security-guidelines.md#keep-all-dependencies-sdks-and-libraries-up-to-date-keep-all-dependencies-sdks-and-libraries-up-to-date
- [definition] Use Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.2 or higher [#use-transport-layer-security-tls-12-or-higher] — Ensure your servers and clients support TLS 1.2 or higher for all communications with PayPal. TLS provides strong encryption and is required for PCI DSS compliance. — https://developer.paypal.com/security-guidelines.md#use-transport-layer-security-tls-12-or-higher-use-transport-layer-security-tls-12-or-higher
- [definition] Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) on your PayPal account [#enable-two-factor-authentication-2fa-on-your-paypal-account] — Enable 2FA to add an extra layer of security to your PayPal account and developer dashboard. 2FA helps prevent unauthorized access, even if your password is compromised. — https://developer.paypal.com/security-guidelines.md#enable-two-factor-authentication-2fa-on-your-paypal-account-enable-two-factor-authentication-2fa-on-your-paypal-account
- [definition] Monitor and log all payment and API activity for suspicious behavior [#monitor-and-log-all-payment-and-api-activity-for-suspicious-behavior] — Implement logging and monitoring for all payment and API activity to detect and respond to suspicious or unauthorized actions. Monitoring helps you identify fraud, abuse, or operational issues quickly. — https://developer.paypal.com/security-guidelines.md#monitor-and-log-all-payment-and-api-activity-for-suspicious-behavior-monitor-and-log-all-payment-and-api-activity-for-suspicious-behavior
- [definition] Follow the principle of least privilege for API credentials [#follow-the-principle-of-least-privilege-for-api-credentials] — Grant only the minimum permissions necessary for each API credential to reduce risk if credentials are compromised. Use separate credentials for different environments and roles. — https://developer.paypal.com/security-guidelines.md#follow-the-principle-of-least-privilege-for-api-credentials-follow-the-principle-of-least-privilege-for-api-credentials
- [definition] Do not log sensitive information such as access tokens or payment details [#do-not-log-sensitive-information-such-as-access-tokens-or-payment-details] — Never log sensitive data such as access tokens, client secrets, or full payment details to prevent accidental exposure. Logging sensitive data can lead to data breaches and non-compliance with PCI DSS. — https://developer.paypal.com/security-guidelines.md#do-not-log-sensitive-information-such-as-access-tokens-or-payment-details-do-not-log-sensitive-information-such-as-access-tokens-or-payment-details
- [definition] Integration-specific security guidelines [#integration-specific-security-guidelines] — PayPal offers several integration paths, each with unique security considerations beyond the general guidelines. The following sections outline specific security requirements, best practices, and code examples for API, SDK, and webhook integrations. — https://developer.paypal.com/security-guidelines.md#integration-specific-security-guidelines-integration-specific-security-guidelines
- [definition] API integration path [#api-integration-path] — The API integration path is for developers who interact directly with PayPal's REST APIs from their server-side applications. — https://developer.paypal.com/security-guidelines.md#api-integration-path-api-integration-path
- [definition] SDK integration path [#sdk-integration-path] — The SDK integration path is for developers who use PayPal's JavaScript SDK to embed payment buttons and checkout flows directly into their web applications. — https://developer.paypal.com/security-guidelines.md#sdk-integration-path-sdk-integration-path
- [definition] Webhook and notification integration [#webhook-and-notification-integration] — Webhook and notification integration is essential for handling asynchronous events from PayPal, such as payment completions, disputes, or subscription updates. This path ensures your server can securely receive and process notifications and that your system trusts only genuine PayPal events. — https://developer.paypal.com/security-guidelines.md#webhook-and-notification-integration-webhook-and-notification-integration
- [definition] Security testing guidelines [#security-testing-guidelines] — Testing your security implementation is critical to ensure your integration is robust against various threats and edge cases. While comprehensive response handling testing is covered in [Handling API responses](/api/handle-api-responses), consider these additional security-specific tests: — https://developer.paypal.com/security-guidelines.md#security-testing-guidelines-security-testing-guidelines
- [definition] PayPal security tools [#paypal-security-tools] — PayPal offers a suite of security tools and features to help secure your integration. — https://developer.paypal.com/security-guidelines.md#paypal-security-tools-paypal-security-tools

- [definition] Go live [#go-live] — 1. Log in to the PayPal Developer Dashboard with your PayPal business account. — https://developer.paypal.com/v5-v6.md#go-live-go-live
- [definition] Troubleshooting [#troubleshooting] — Troubleshoot common errors that you might encounter when upgrading from v5 to v6. — https://developer.paypal.com/v5-v6.md#troubleshooting-troubleshooting
- [definition] SDK does not initialize [#sdk-does-not-initialize] — If `window.paypal.createInstance` is undefined, the core script has not finished loading. Make sure your initialization code runs inside the `onload` callback on the script tag. — https://developer.paypal.com/v5-v6.md#sdk-does-not-initialize-sdk-does-not-initialize
- [definition] Buttons do not appear [#buttons-do-not-appear] — v6 buttons are hidden by default. If nothing shows on your page, check these items: 1. — https://developer.paypal.com/v5-v6.md#buttons-do-not-appear-buttons-do-not-appear
- [definition] Client token fetch fails [#client-token-fetch-fails] — If your `/paypal-api/auth/browser-safe-client-token` endpoint returns a 401 error, check your server credentials. Common causes: 1. — https://developer.paypal.com/v5-v6.md#client-token-fetch-fails-client-token-fetch-fails
- [definition] `createOrder` does not return an order ID [#createorder-does-not-return-an-order-id] — In v5, `createOrder` returned a value directly to the button config. In v6, the order ID Promise is passed to `session.start()` as the second argument; it's not returned from `createOrder` itself. — https://developer.paypal.com/v5-v6.md#createorder-does-not-return-an-order-id-createorder-does-not-return-an-order-id

## GraphQL Request Batching
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/request_batching/>

- [snippet] GraphQL Request Batching: HTTP — `HTTP` — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/request_batching/#graphql-request-batching
- [snippet] Responses: [ — `[` — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/request_batching/#responses
- [snippet] Responses: [ — `[` — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/request_batching/#responses
- [snippet] When to use Request Batching: query MultiQuery { — `query MultiQuery {` — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/request_batching/#when-to-use-request-batching
- [snippet] When to use Request Batching: mutation MultiMutation( — `mutation MultiMutation(` — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/request_batching/#when-to-use-request-batching
- [definition] GraphQL Request Batching — We are working on an "extension" of GraphQL at Braintree to allow clients to execute a series of GraphQL queries in a single HTTP request, and optionally share variables between them. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/request_batching/#graphql-request-batching
- [definition] Responses — Just as the request is a list of regular GraphQL request payloads, the response is a list of regular GraphQL response payloads, in the same order. For instance, if everything goes well, the above request would return something like this: — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/request_batching/#responses
- [definition] When to use Request Batching — Request batching should only be used in specific scenarios, namely when you need to mix mutations and queries in a single request, and/or when you need to pass variables from one to the other. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/request_batching/#when-to-use-request-batching
- [definition] Prior Art — This form of request batching has already been popularized by some GraphQL server implementations, for instance and [Sangria](https://sangria-graphql.github.io/learn/#batch-executor). — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/request_batching/#prior-art
- [definition] More Considerations and Limitations — This is a non-exhaustive list; it may change in future as we add functionality. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/request_batching/#more-considerations-and-limitations
- [definition] All queries will be executed, even if there are errors. — As the previous errors example shows, all queries are executed even when previous queries have "failed". This is because GraphQL doesn't really have a binary representation of failure. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/request_batching/#all-queries-will-be-executed-even-if-there-are-errors
- [definition] All queries are executed sequentially. — While we do expect clients to see slight performance improvements from this feature due to less overall HTTP round-trips, the underlying queries will be executed sequentially. So every query you add to your list will introduce that much extra time to your overall response. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/request_batching/#all-queries-are-executed-sequentially
- [definition] Only scalar values can be exported. — This is actually a hard requirement due to the distinction between GraphQL input and output types. Even if we supported exporting a non-scalar field, it wouldn't be usable as input in subsequent queries. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/request_batching/#only-scalar-values-can-be-exported
- [definition] Exported variables are interoperable with passed-in variables. — There's nothing stopping you from referencing both exported variables and those in the `variables` object of your query. Just note that variables in the `variables` object will override exported ones in the event of a conflict. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/request_batching/#exported-variables-are-interoperable-with-passed-in-variables
- [definition] Exporting fields that are under a list node will only export the last value encountered. — We haven't decided how to support accumulating values into a list variable yet (although we're exploring some options). For now it will just override the exported variable for each result in the list, which is probably not what you want. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/request_batching/#exporting-fields-that-are-under-a-list-node-will-only-export-the-last-value-encountered
- [definition] Authentication applies to all queries. — The examples we used here conveniently all accept public/private key basic authentication. However, there may be cases where different query fields will expect different authentication, which is not currently supported. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/request_batching/#authentication-applies-to-all-queries
- [definition] Motivation — One of our goals designing the Braintree GraphQL API has been to break down our existing API features into smaller, composable pieces. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/graphql/guides/request_batching/#motivation

## Must Knows Before Onboarding to SCIM @ Braintree
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/control-panel/users-roles/scim/scim-faq>

- [definition] Must Knows Before Onboarding to SCIM @ Braintree — Please read through the below sections to learn the what, why, and how of SCIM, as well as various troubleshooting and FAQ's about SCIM and SCIM at Braintree. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/control-panel/users-roles/scim/scim-faq#must-knows-before-onboarding-to-scim-braintree
- [definition] What is SCIM? — SCIM, or the System for Cross-domain Identity Management specification, is an open standard for managing user identity information. SCIM provides a defined schema for representing users and groups and a RESTful API to run CRUD operations on those user and group resources. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/control-panel/users-roles/scim/scim-faq#what-is-scim
- [definition] Why SCIM? — We have many merchants. You have many users — hundreds, if not thousands — all of whom need to be onboarded, offboarded, modified, or suspended. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/control-panel/users-roles/scim/scim-faq#why-scim
- [definition] How does SCIM work? — Essentially, when we set up SCIM for you, we do some data setup on our side, and then we give you an access token for your IDP to interact with us. Consider this similar to an API key or password that helps their service make requests that modify your users or groups on your behalf. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/control-panel/users-roles/scim/scim-faq#how-does-scim-work

## Disputing Chargebacks
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/disputing-chargebacks>

- [definition] Disputing Chargebacks — If one of your customers issues a chargeback through their bank, you have the chance to dispute it and win back the funds. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/disputing-chargebacks#disputing-chargebacks
- [definition] When to accept — Merchants typically accept chargebacks if: - The transaction amount is minor enough that it doesn’t justify the work of submitting evidence - The transaction is known to be fraudulent - A refund is warranted and the chargeback can be accepted in lieu of issuing a manual refund — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/disputing-chargebacks#when-to-accept
- [definition] When to dispute — Merchants typically dispute chargebacks if: - They are confident the transaction was legitimate - They have compelling evidence against the chargeback - The disputed amount is large enough to justify the work of submitting evidence — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/disputing-chargebacks#when-to-dispute
- [definition] Submitting evidence — Every chargeback is different, so the evidence you provide will vary depending on the reason for the chargeback and the documents you have available. We recommend keeping records of all transactions, so you are prepared in the event that a chargeback does happen. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/disputing-chargebacks#submitting-evidence
- [definition] PayPal disputes — PayPal disputes can be managed in your Braintree Control Panel and your PayPal Resolution Center. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/disputing-chargebacks#paypal-disputes
- [definition] Refunds — Sometimes, customers may request a refund from you directly while simultaneously issuing a chargeback with their bank. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/disputing-chargebacks#refunds
- [definition] Pre-arbitrations — While you can dispute pre-arbitrations, it's been our experience that merchants rarely win these cases without the introduction of new and compelling evidence. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/disputing-chargebacks#pre-arbitrations

## Reducing Chargebacks
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/reducing-chargebacks>

- [definition] Reducing Chargebacks — While it’s impossible to prevent chargebacks entirely, there are steps you can take to significantly reduce their frequency. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/reducing-chargebacks#reducing-chargebacks
- [definition] Collect customer information — Collect as much customer information as possible with each transaction. The billing street address, billing postal code, and the CVV are particularly important. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/reducing-chargebacks#collect-customer-information
- [definition] Be upfront with your customers — Make sure that your site's terms and conditions are easy to find and understand. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/reducing-chargebacks#be-upfront-with-your-customers
- [definition] Be accessible — Make it easy for your customers to contact you if they have questions or issues. We recommend that you clearly display your contact information on each page of your website. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/reducing-chargebacks#be-accessible
- [definition] Provide your service or product as soon as possible — The sooner your product or service is delivered to your customers, the less likely they are to be dissatisfied with their purchase. Make sure you make shipping timelines visible for customers so their expectations are set appropriately. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/reducing-chargebacks#provide-your-service-or-product-as-soon-as-possible
- [definition] Make sure your subscriptions are opt-in — If you offer your customers a free trial period before they start a subscription or recurring billing service, always make sure to give them the option to opt-out of the paid service. We do not recommend collecting customer payment information for the free trial. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/reducing-chargebacks#make-sure-your-subscriptions-are-opt-in
- [definition] Provide refunds — The most effective way to prevent chargebacks from customers who are dissatisfied with a product or service is to establish an easy and efficient refund process. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/reducing-chargebacks#provide-refunds
- [definition] Use a recognizable descriptor — Your [descriptor](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/control-panel/transactions/descriptors) controls the way your company name appears on your customer’s bank statements. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/reducing-chargebacks#use-a-recognizable-descriptor
- [definition] Be proactive internally — There are some internal processes you can implement to reduce the frequency and probability of chargebacks. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/reducing-chargebacks#be-proactive-internally
- [definition] Use a CAPTCHA on your site — A CAPTCHA is a program or system designed to tell the difference between human and machine input. Having a CAPTCHA on your site can help prevent carding attacks – and the subsequent chargebacks due to fraudulent charges. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/reducing-chargebacks#use-a-captcha-on-your-site
- [definition] Use our fraud tools — Less fraudulent charges for your customers mean fewer chargebacks for you. We offer varying levels of fraud protection to meet your business’s needs; see our [fraud tools guide](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/fraud-tools/overview) for more information. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/chargebacks-retrievals/reducing-chargebacks#use-our-fraud-tools

## Two-Factor Authentication
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/control-panel-security/two-factor-authentication>

- [definition] Two-Factor Authentication — Two-factor authentication (2FA) is an extra layer of security that can be added to a user in the Control Panel, making it more difficult for unauthorized users to access your gateway. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/control-panel-security/two-factor-authentication#two-factor-authentication
- [definition] How to enable 2FA — Starting in September 2023, 2FA is required for all Braintree users, and each user must enable 2FA to access Control Panel. For any user who does not have 2FA enabled, a 2FA set-up assistant will automatically appear after the user logs in. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/control-panel-security/two-factor-authentication#how-to-enable-2fa
- [definition] Setting up a Hardware Security Key — When 2FA is enabled on a user's account, they can then register a WebAuthn U2F compatible security key with their account: 1. Log into the [Control Panel](https://www.braintreegateway.com/login) 2. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/control-panel-security/two-factor-authentication#setting-up-a-hardware-security-key
- [definition] Signing in with 2FA — Once 2FA is enabled on a user account, every time they sign into the Control Panel they'll be prompted for their second factor in the following order: 1. Hardware Security Key (if registered) 2. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/control-panel-security/two-factor-authentication#signing-in-with-2fa
- [definition] Managing a Web Authentication (WebAuthn) Security Key — 1. Log into the [Control Panel](https://www.braintreegateway.com/login) 2. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/control-panel-security/two-factor-authentication#managing-a-web-authentication-webauthn-security-key
- [definition] How to Temporarily Disable 2FA for a user — If one of your users is locked out of the Control Panel, or is unable to access their mobile device at the time of login, your Braintree Account Admin will need to disable 2FA for that user's account. The user will be prompted to set up 2FA the next time they log in: — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/control-panel-security/two-factor-authentication#how-to-temporarily-disable-2fa-for-a-user
- [definition] How to reset 2FA — Starting in September 2023, the users won't be able to disable 2FA for themselves. Instead, there will be the option to reset 2FA within **My User** from the drop-down menu. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/control-panel-security/two-factor-authentication#how-to-reset-2fa
- [definition] Authenticator Apps — Braintree’s 2FA implementation is compatible with most Time-based One-Time Password (TOTP) applications. ## Rolling reserves
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves>

- [parameter] **Collection method**: Rolling reserve=Percentage of daily sales, ongoing; Risk reserve=Percentage of daily sales, up to a cap — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#reserve-types
- [parameter] **Release**: Rolling reserve=Automatic after the holding period (30–120 days); Risk reserve=On drawdown or account closure — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#reserve-types
- [parameter] **Balance ceiling**: Rolling reserve=None (balance fluctuates daily); Risk reserve=Hard cap (for example, $5,000) — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#reserve-types
- [parameter] **Cash flow impact**: Rolling reserve=Incremental and ongoing; Risk reserve=Incremental until the cap is reached, then none — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#reserve-types
- [parameter] **Best suited for**: Rolling reserve=Standard-risk merchants with ongoing volume; Risk reserve=Moderate-risk merchants that require an exposure limit or cap — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#reserve-types

- [parameter] Jan 12: Gross sales=$11,000; Reserve held (5%)=$100; Cumulative balance=$5,000; Notes=Braintree withholds only $100 to reach the cap. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#example
- [parameter] Jan 13: Gross sales=$9,000; Reserve held (5%)=$0; Cumulative balance=$5,000; Notes=The reserve balance is at the cap, so Braintree withholds no funds. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#example
- [parameter] Jan 20: Gross sales=$7,000; Reserve held (5%)=$200; Cumulative balance=$5,000; Notes=A chargeback reduced the balance to $4,800, so withholding resumes. Braintree withholds $200 to return the reserve balance to the cap amount. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#example
- [parameter] Cap amount: The maximum dollar amount that a capped reserve can hold. Once the balance reaches this amount, Braintree withholds no further funds. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#key-terms
- [parameter] Effective date: The date a reserve configuration takes effect. Changes apply prospectively and don't retroactively affect funds already held. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#key-terms
- [parameter] Gross sales: The total value of transactions settled on a given day, before deductions for refunds, chargebacks, or fees. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#key-terms
- [parameter] Holding period: The number of calendar days that reserved funds are held before automatic release. Braintree counts calendar days, not business days. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#key-terms
- [parameter] Reserve balance: The total amount currently held in reserve for a merchant account. Braintree tracks this separately from risk-held balances. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#key-terms
- [parameter] Reserve held: The dollar amount withheld from a daily disbursement and added to the reserve balance. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#key-terms
- [parameter] Reserve released: The dollar amount returned to a merchant as part of a daily disbursement when the holding period expires. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#key-terms
- [parameter] Risk hold: A separate operational hold on disbursements that a specific risk event triggers. Risk holds operate independently from rolling and capped reserves. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#key-terms
- [definition] Rolling reserves — If a merchant can't cover its obligations, such as chargebacks from dissatisfied customers, refunds on undelivered goods, or fraud. Reserves are the main tool that Braintree uses to manage this exposure. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#rolling-reserves
- [definition] Reserve types — The following table describes the reserve types that Braintree uses. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#reserve-types
- [definition] Common features of reserves — A few behaviors apply across both rolling and capped reserves. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#common-features-of-reserves
- [definition] Rolling reserves — A rolling reserve holds a fixed percentage of a merchant's gross daily sales for a set number of calendar days. When the holding period for a given day's funds expires, Braintree automatically releases those funds in the next disbursement. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#rolling-reserves
- [definition] Risk reserves — With a risk (or *capped*) reserve, Braintree stops collecting when the total reserve balance reaches a specified cap amount. If the balance later falls below the cap, collection resumes automatically. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#risk-reserves
- [definition] Opting out of a reserve requirement — To opt out of a reserve requirement, set the percentage and holding period to 0 (zero) with a future effective date. After that date, Braintree withholds no new funds. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#opting-out-of-a-reserve-requirement
- [definition] Key terms — The following table defines key terms about reserves. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves#key-terms

- [parameter] Adjustments: The net change to a merchant’s reserve balance and, if applicable, collections for a given disbursement, as reported in the DFR. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#key-terms
- [parameter] Cap amount: The maximum dollar amount that a capped reserve can hold. Once the balance reaches this amount, no further funds are withheld. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#key-terms
- [parameter] Collections: Funds a merchant owes Braintree — for example, from excessive chargebacks — that are netted against the disbursement before payout. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#key-terms
- [parameter] DFR (Daily Funding Report): The report that summarizes a merchant account’s daily disbursement activity, including reserve holds, releases, and adjustments. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#key-terms
- [parameter] Disbursement: The net amount transferred to, or debited from, a merchant’s linked bank account for a given day. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#key-terms
- [parameter] Effective date: The date a reserve configuration change takes effect. Changes apply prospectively and don’t retroactively affect funds already held. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#key-terms
- [parameter] Gross sales: The total value of transactions settled on a given day, before deductions for refunds, chargebacks, or fees. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#key-terms
- [parameter] Holding period: The number of calendar days that reserved funds are held before automatic release. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#key-terms
- [parameter] Reserve balance: The total amount currently held in reserve for a merchant account, tracked separately from risk-held balances. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#key-terms
- [parameter] Reserve held: The dollar amount withheld from a daily disbursement and added to the reserve balance. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#key-terms
- [parameter] Reserve released: The dollar amount returned to a merchant as part of a daily disbursement when the holding period expires. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#key-terms
- [parameter] Risk hold: A separate operational hold on disbursements triggered by a specific risk event, independent of rolling and capped reserves. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#key-terms
- [definition] Disbursements — Daily disbursement is the net amount that Braintree transfers to the merchant's linked bank account after applying all deductions and additions for that day. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#disbursements
- [definition] How reserves affect your disbursement — A disbursement isn't gross sales minus refunds, chargebacks, and fees. When a reserve is active, Braintree also subtracts the amount held for that day's reserve and adds back any previously held funds scheduled to be released that day. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#how-reserves-affect-your-disbursement
- [definition] Rolling reserve — When a rolling reserve is active, Braintree calculates the daily disbursement as follows: **Daily Disbursement = Gross Sales − Refunds − Chargebacks − Fees − Reserve Held + Reserve Released** — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#rolling-reserve
- [definition] Capped reserve — The capped (risk) reserve formula depends on whether the current reserve balance has reached the cap. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#capped-reserve
- [definition] Rolling reserve example — Configuration: 5% reserve, 30-day holding period, effective January 1. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#rolling-reserve-example
- [definition] Capped reserve example — Configuration: 5% reserve, $5,000 cap, effective January 1. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#capped-reserve-example
- [definition] Disbursements under risk holds and collections — Rolling and capped reserves operate independently of risk holds and collections. However, when either is active alongside a reserve, the disbursement amount and the Daily Funding Report (DFR) reflect that interaction differently. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#disbursements-under-risk-holds-and-collections
- [definition] Merchant under a risk hold — When Braintree holds a merchant’s disbursement because of a risk event — for example, a carding attack — reserve calculations continue as normal, and the full disbursement amount is held rather than paid out: — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#merchant-under-a-risk-hold
- [definition] Merchant under collections — When a merchant owes Braintree money — for example, because of excessive chargebacks — Braintree nets the owed amount from the disbursement before payout. Reserve calculations are based on the pre-netting amount. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#merchant-under-collections
- [definition] Negative disbursements — If refunds, chargebacks, fees, and reserve holds together exceed gross sales plus any reserve releases for the day, the disbursement can be negative. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#negative-disbursements
- [definition] Zero gross-sales days — On a day with no transaction activity: - **No reserve is held** — there are no gross sales to calculate a hold against. - **Releases still occur** — any previously held funds scheduled to release that day are still included in the disbursement. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#zero-gross-sales-days
- [definition] Weekend and holiday releases — Release dates that fall on a weekend or holiday shift to the next business day. On the following business day, a merchant may see 2–3 separate release line items in the DFR — one for each calendar day whose holding period expired during the non-business days. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#weekend-and-holiday-releases
- [definition] Configuration changes mid-cycle — Reserve configurations use an effective-date model: - **Existing holds aren’t affected.** Funds already held under a previous configuration keep their original holding period and release date. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#configuration-changes-mid-cycle
- [definition] Capped reserve: cap amount reduced — If the cap amount is lowered below the current reserve balance, Braintree releases the excess as a “Reserve Released” line item in the next disbursement. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#capped-reserve-cap-amount-reduced
- [definition] Opting out of a reserve — To remove a reserve, set the percentage and holding period to zero with a future effective date: - **After the effective date** , no new funds are withheld. - **Scheduled releases continue** — any funds already held are released on their original schedule. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/risk-and-security/underwriting/reserves/disbursements#opting-out-of-a-reserve

## Processing
<https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/braintree-marketplace/processing>

- [definition] Processing — If you're a new merchant looking for a marketplace solution, — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/braintree-marketplace/processing#processing
- [definition] Service fees — A service fee allows you to take a portion of your sub-merchant's transaction revenue and route those funds to your master merchant account. The remainder will be disbursed to your sub-merchant. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/braintree-marketplace/processing#service-fees
- [definition] Escrow — Escrow allows you to withhold your sub-merchants’ disbursements and release them at a later date. This can help mitigate financial risks when a sub-merchant fails to deliver a service or product. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/braintree-marketplace/processing#escrow
- [definition] Refunds — Refunds work a little differently depending on whether or not the funds are being held in escrow. If they are in escrow, the full amount of the transaction will be **pulled from escrow** and returned to the customer. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/braintree-marketplace/processing#refunds
- [definition] Disputes — We will contact you if a is issued against one of your sub-merchant’s transactions. Funds for the chargeback, along with any associated fees, will be deducted from your master merchant bank account. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/braintree-marketplace/processing#disputes
- [definition] Collecting funds from your sub-merchants — Because refunds and chargebacks pull funds from your bank account and not your sub-merchants’ funding sources, here are some ways you can recoup those funds: - Increase your service fees to mitigate losses due to high refund or chargeback rates from sub-merchants. — https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/braintree-marketplace/processing#collecting-funds-from-your-sub-merchants
